endorsements.quote: Instead, the extent of validation, human oversight, governance, and post-implementation monitoring should be determined by the intended clinical use, the potential impact on patient care, and the associated level of risk.

Each deployed AI system should have clearly defined clinical and operational ownership, supported by appropriate documentation, version control, audit trails, access management, cybersecurity, change management and corrective and preventive action (CAPA) processes.
Local verification should confirm reliable integration between whole-slide scanners, image management systems (IMS),
Successful implementation requires verification of interoperability across the entire digital pathology ecosystem rather than validation of the AI algorithm alone [ 11].
Oversight by appropriately trained and experienced pathologists, with active evaluation of AI outputs rather than passive acceptance, mitigates the risks associated with automation bias.
AI should augment rather than replace professional judgement, and responsibility for diagnostic decisions remains with the reporting pathologist.

Training, applicable to all laboratory staff, including residents, should extend beyond the operation of the AI software to include its intended use, limitations, potential failure modes and circumstances requiring mandatory human review.

Continuous monitoring should assess whether AI performance remains acceptable in the local clinical environment and trigger further investigation or revalidation when clinically significant changes in performance are identified.

Investigation should include incident classification, assessment of clinical impact, root-cause analysis, implementation of corrective and preventive actions, verification of their effectiveness and ongoing monitoring.
Maintaining an up-todate inventory of deployed AI systems, including software versions, intended use and implementation status, facilitates governance, traceability and regulatory compliance.
Periodic refresher training should be considered following major software updates, workflow modifications or changes in the intended clinical use of the AI system.

Minor software patches or security updates may require only limited verification, whereas algorithm retraining, major software revisions, scanner or stainer replacement, or other significant technical changes should trigger proportionate repeat verification or revalida tion before clinical redeployment.
Laboratories may choose to use regulatory-approved AI outside the manufacturer's intended use or implement AI in a "silent" mode to evaluate performance before clinical deployment.

Technical indicators, including scanner performance and software failures, together with governance measures such as manual override frequency, incident reporting and audit outcomes, should also form part of routine monitor ing.

Implementation should comply with applicable national and international regulatory frameworks, including IVDR, FDA, CE marking, UKCA, the European Union AI Act, ISO 15189 and ISO 13485, where relevant [ 10, 22].

Safe deployment depends on effective collaboration between manufacturers and laboratories, with clearly defined responsibilities for software updates, technical support, incident investigation, and performance monitoring.

unlisted_practices: Deploy AI systems only for the manufacturer's intended clinical use, and subject any off-label use to explicit declaration, additional governance, validation and institutional approval proportionate to risk.
Document in diagnostic reports the use and scope of AI assistance, stating that final interpretation and diagnostic accountability rest with the reporting pathologist.
Verify that AI systems perform robustly across local pre-analytical variability such as folds, air bubbles, out-of-focus regions and staining variation.
Validate stain normalisation and other image pre-processing for the intended AI application before implementing it.
Define contingency plans for AI system failure or temporary unavailability.
Ensure de-identification, contractual safeguards, cybersecurity and legal compliance (e.g. GDPR) when transferring images or metadata to external vendors or cloud platforms.
Integrate AI activities into existing laboratory quality management systems with specific training and resource provision.
Define local procedures specifying when AI outputs may be accepted, when mandatory human review is required, and how discrepancies are managed.
Prespecify the primary performance metric and acceptance criteria for local verification before reviewing cases, and defer or suspend deployment if criteria are not met.
Adopt recognised interoperability standards such as DICOM and HL7/FHIR where supported.
Include AI in external quality assessment where available.
Engage multidisciplinary teams early to agree on interpretation, reporting thresholds and clinical integration of AI-derived biomarker results.
Formally assess changes to algorithm, scanner or staining protocol during clinical trials that use AI, with version control and auditability.

screen.reason: This is a guidance and governance framework paper providing recommendations for pathology laboratories on the implementation, verification, governance, and continuous monitoring of AI systems.
